title: As if today (I.23)
hook: act in each thing as if you were to die today
tomorrow: how do you change without burning out by week two?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misery of being human: nobody, not even a king or a pope, has everything their way, and the body's plain needs prove it. The line was everyone has sorrow.

Last practice before a move. Last shift before someone retires. Last dinner with everyone home before somebody leaves for college. People act differently on a last time. They say the thank-you. They take the photo. They don't spend the hour on their phone. Nobody has to tell them to. The Imitation asks for that kind of attention on ordinary days, and its reason is blunt. In the morning, it says, consider that you may not reach evening; in the evening, don't promise yourself the morning.
screen: `THE LAST TIME CHANGES THINGS.` → `YOU MAY NOT REACH EVENING.` → `DON'T PROMISE YOURSELF THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-three of book one is about death, and it's gentler than its subject. Practical, not morbid. Today a person is here, it says; tomorrow, gone, and once out of sight, soon out of mind. Then the line the day is named for: in every act and every thought, order yourself as if you were to die today. Notice what it doesn't ask for. Not fear. If your conscience were clear, the book says, you wouldn't fear death much; it's better to avoid sin than to run from death. And it gives a practical warning: don't leave to friends and family, after you're gone, what you can do for your own soul now. Do good while you have time. One more line, and it's the kindest. The chapter calls happy the person who keeps the hour of death before their eyes and gets ready for it every day. But ready doesn't mean packing a bag. In this chapter it means not leaving the apology for later, or the call, or the kindness. Some people hear a line like this and think: you only live once, so go wild. The Imitation means nearly the opposite. Not recklessness, and not gloom. It's last-practice attention, turned on an ordinary Tuesday: the next conversation, the next chore, done as if nothing came after it.
screen: `TODAY HERE, TOMORROW GONE.` · `AS IF YOU WERE TO DIE TODAY.` · `A CLEAR CONSCIENCE FEARS LESS.` · `DO GOOD WHILE YOU HAVE TIME.` · then, large: `AS IF TODAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one message you've been putting off: a thank-you, an apology, a plain I'm proud of you. Write it now, in simple words, as if there won't be a better time, and hold it until the sit ends. Short is fine. If you pray, you can offer the person to God as you write.
As if today. The Imitation's counsel: order each act and each thought as if this were the last day, with a clear conscience.
Keep this one: as if today, since tomorrow isn't promised and today is right here. See you soon.

howItsDone: Many Catholics examine their conscience each night, and the Church prays for a holy death; the Imitation's chapter on death is read as a call to live each day well rather than to fear.

notes: Imitation I.23 paraphrased: very quickly it will be over with thee here; today man is, tomorrow he is gone, and out of sight is quickly out of mind; in every deed and thought so order thyself as if thou wert to die today; with a good conscience thou wouldst not much fear death; better to avoid sin than flee death; blessed is he who has the hour of death always before his eyes and daily prepares to die; in the morning think thou mayst not reach evening, at evening promise not thyself the morning; trust not in friends and kinsfolk nor put off thy soul's welfare to the future. Confirm.
'Memento mori' is not a phrase in the Imitation; it is used only in the games as the Latin name for this kind of reflection, and the original note says so.
